transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2025-07-15 16:00 PDT
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Nina Torres (Redwood CSM); Maya Singh (Omega Health CISO), Ethan Park (Sr. Security Engineer), Lena Ortiz (Compliance Manager)

Summary: Security and BCDR review focused on incident response, RTO/RPO targets, uptime/SLA guarantees, escalation paths and integration with customer's on-call tools.

Topics: SOC 2/ISO attestations; RBAC/SSO and SAML integration; audit logs and retention; encryption / KMS key custody; Incident response runbook; BCDR failover strategy (RTO/RPO); SLA uptime and credits; escalation and PagerDuty integration.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick check — can you hear us okay?
[00:08] Maya (Omega Health - CISO): Yep, loud and clear. Thanks Alex. We wanted to focus today on incident response, BCDR and how your SLA and escalation process would fit into our vendor risk program.
[00:18] Alex: Perfect, that's the plan. I'll kick off with a brief overview then Samir will dive into the technical bits and runbooks. Nina will cover SLA amendment language and support tiers.
[00:28] Samir (Redwood SE): Hi all. Just to set expectations, Redwood supports hosted, dedicated and private deployments; the BCDR posture differs slightly by mode. For hosted we have multi-region active/passive with automated failover, dedicated gives you reserved capacity in a region plus cross-region failover options, and private is customer-controlled — we provide the orchestration.
[00:45] Ethan (Omega Health - Sr Sec Eng): Quick clarifying question — when you say automated failover for hosted, what are the typical RTO and RPO numbers?
[00:54] Samir: Good question. For our hosted tier we target an RTO of under 30 minutes for critical control plane incidents and under 10 minutes for worker region failovers where the route is simple; RPO varies — we aim for sub-1 minute for live request KV cache/state for short-lived sessions, but for sessionless APIs RPO is near-zero because requests are stateless. That said, RPO depends on caching policies and customer-configured TTLs.
[01:22] Maya: Sub-1 minute for KV cache seems optimistic. Do you have real-world benchmarks or runbooks we can review?
[01:29] Samir: We do. We'll share the incident response runbook and a condensed failover playbook. Real-world numbers from our internal incidents show region-level re-routing within 6-8 minutes on average for recent exercises; control plane incidents can take longer if we need state reconciliation.
[01:42] Lena (Compliance): Is there a formal post-incident RCA process and SLT involvement? We need timelines for initial notif, regular updates, and an RCA deliverable.
[01:51] Nina (Redwood CSM): Yes — our SLA and incident response policy includes 15-minute acknowledgement for Sev1 incidents, regular updates (every 30 min) until mitigation, and a full RCA within 5 business days for major incidents. We can align notification paths with Omega Health's escalation matrix.
[02:07] Maya: On the legal side we need concrete RTO/RPO in the contract. If the hosted defaults are variable, can you offer a contractual SLA with explicit RTO/RPO options?
[02:17] Alex: We can — we typically offer tiers. For Dedicated we provide tighter RTO guarantees because you have reserved capacity, and for Private deployments we can scope a customer-specific RTO/RPO. Nina will draft SLA amendment language with example credits.
[02:30] Ethan: About audit logs — how long do you retain security/audit logs and what granularity? We need tamper-evident logs for access and admin actions for at least 1 year, ideally 3 years.
[02:40] Samir: Our default audit log retention for hosted is 90 days in the console, but we do export to long-term storage on request; we support S3 export or integrations with SIEMs and can retain up to 3 years if contracted. Logs are write-once-read-many and use integrity checks; we can provide hash-based attestations.
[02:58] Maya: KMS — who holds the master keys? We have strict data custody requirements and may require customer-managed keys (BYOK) for production.
[03:07] Samir: Redwood supports both service-managed keys and customer-managed keys in major cloud KMS providers. For Private deployments customers can hold keys in their HSM/KMS. For hosted with CMK, we integrate with the customer's KMS and enforce key rotation policies. We'll share the KMS integration guide.
[03:27] Lena: Is metadata or logs ever stored unencrypted?
[03:31] Samir: No — at rest all customer data and logs are encrypted. Metadata that is required for routing is redacted or hashed and stored encrypted as well.
[03:39] Maya: Ok, escalation process specifics — we use PagerDuty. Can Redwood integrate so that Sev1 alerts create incidents in our PD and notify our SLT?
[03:48] Nina: Yes — we have a PagerDuty integration and can configure webhook-based incident creation. For enterprise customers we do bi-directional routing so updates in Redwood trigger PD updates, and vice versa. We'll need your PD service key and routing rules.
[04:03] Ethan: Great. Also interested in on-call rotations and single point of contact — will Redwood provide a dedicated account manager plus an on-call engineer for critical incidents?
[04:14] Alex: For enterprise customers we offer a named technical account lead and 24/7 on-call support for Sev1s. The on-call rotation is Redwood internal; we provide contact info and escalation ladders, and can agree on SLT notification thresholds.
[04:29] Maya: About SLAs — what uptime % do you guarantee and what are the credit boundaries? We need to map to our vendor risk reporting.
[04:38] Nina: Our standard hosted SLA is 99.9% availability for the API surface, with credits starting at anything below 99.9, escalating credit percentages for below 99.5 and 99.0. For Dedicated we can move to 99.95 or 99.99 for an additional commitment. We'll share an SLA table in the follow-up.
[04:56] Ethan: How do you measure availability? Is it from the control plane or from the public API endpoints in our region?
[05:03] Samir: Availability is measured from our synthetic checks hitting the public API endpoints in the customer's primary region, plus internal health metrics of route tables and worker pools. We'll provide the exact monitoring definitions in the SLA appendix.
[05:16] Lena: For audit purposes we need clock-synced timestamps on logs and RFC3339 format; also an exportable digest for long-term storage.
[05:25] Samir: We use RFC3339 timestamps and can provide signed digests of exported logs for tamper evidence.
[05:31] Maya: Let's talk incident classification — what's a Sev1 versus Sev2?
[05:36] Nina: By our definitions, Sev1 is system down or data-loss impacting production in-scope workloads; Sev2 is degraded performance materially affecting production (e.g., sustained latency increase beyond SLO); Sev3 is functional but non-critical issues. We can align definitions with Omega's SOC matrix.
[05:49] Maya: And what about BCDR exercises — do you run periodic failover drills and can customers observe?
[05:55] Samir: Yes — we run quarterly chaos/drill exercises internally. For enterprise customers we offer joint failover exercises annually or on-demand for a scoped window; customers can nominate observers or participate actively. We can also run a mini failover demo for your team.
[06:09] Ethan: For private deployment, is the responsibility split clear? We need a runbook that shows customer tasks vs Redwood tasks during failover.
[06:17] Samir: Absolutely — the runbook clarifies ownership: customer owns network, KMS keys (if BYOK), and VPC-level routing for private; Redwood owns the runtime orchestration and data-plane processes. We'll provide a matrix.
[06:29] Alex: Quick note on timelines — if we agree to Dedicated or Private we can include explicit RTO/RPO in contract and run a technical onboarding to test the measures.
[06:38] Maya: Cool. One of our constraints is data residency — certain PHI data must stay in US-east only. How do you ensure routing and model variants respect residency?
[06:47] Samir: We support region pinning and routing policies at the customer level. For hosted customers we can enforce region-only processing for specific routes or models. For extra assurance, Dedicated capacity in-region or Private deployment is recommended.
[06:59] Lena: During incidents, what customer-facing communications do you provide? We need templates and cadence.
[07:05] Nina: We provide an initial incident acknowledgement within 15 minutes for Sev1s, then status updates every 30 minutes, with a post-incident RCA within 5 business days. We'll provide message templates and a runbook for communications.
[07:16] Maya: Role-based access control — we need fine-grained RBAC so only select users can manage keys, change routing, and approve failovers. Can roles be mapped to our SAML groups?
[07:26] Samir: Yes — RBAC maps to SAML/SCIM provisioning. We support custom roles and can restrict actions like 'modify routing', 'manage keys', 'initiate failover'. We'll share the RBAC matrix.
[07:37] Ethan: Regarding the KV cache mention earlier, how much state do you persist and is there a way to backfill or replay if cache is lost?
[07:45] Samir: The KV cache is ephemeral for latency reasons; for critical session state we recommend persisting to customer-managed stores (Redis, etc.). We can provide guidance on de-coupling session-affine state. Cache misses may increase latency but not cause data loss.
[07:58] Maya: Any encryption in transit details? TLS versions and mutual TLS options?
[08:03] Samir: All traffic is TLS 1.2+; we support TLS 1.3 and mTLS for private deployments. We can require client certs for private endpoints.
[08:13] Lena: For compliance we may want signed attestations of key rotation and access. Can you provide audit trail extracts?
[08:19] Samir: Yes, we can produce audit extracts showing key usage, rotations, and admin actions, with HMAC-signed digests.
[08:26] Maya: Back to SLA credits — what if root cause is a third-party cloud provider outage? How does that affect credits?
[08:34] Nina: Our SLA has carve-outs for force majeure and major cloud provider outages if they are verified and out of our control; however we still run mitigation and provide transparency. For enterprise contracts we can negotiate shared responsibility exceptions.
[08:48] Alex: We'd also propose a joint tabletop exercise to validate the escalation paths. That helps both teams.
[08:54] Maya: Yes, we like that. We'll want observers from our legal and ops teams for the tabletop.
[08:59] Ethan: One more technical Q — do you have runbooks for DR that include database snapshots, model weights versioning, and rollback steps?
[09:07] Samir: We version models and store immutable model artifacts; our DR playbooks include rollback and re-deploy steps and snapshots for critical config. For customers who require it, we support snapshot export to customer-controlled storage.
[09:20] Maya: Let's capture the main decisions: 1) Redwood to send SOC2/ISO & runbooks, 2) schedule BCDR demo, 3) Redwood drafts SLA amendment with RTO/RPO options, 4) Omega to share PagerDuty contacts.
[09:33] Alex: Yup, that's the list. Any other questions?
[09:36] Lena: A small nit — what is your policy on data deletion and proof of deletion? For our regs we need certs that data was purged.
[09:44] Samir: We support certified data deletion workflows with retention windows; we can produce deletion attestations and provide proof-of-deletion logs.
[09:51] Maya: For the SOC2 report, will it show how you do change management for the runtime? We need to see the control matrix.
[09:58] Alex: Yes — the SOC2 Type II includes control narratives around deployment change management, code review, and release processes. We'll share the report and control matrix.
[10:08] Ethan: Ok thanks. On the PagerDuty integration, one more detail: can incidents be auto-created from Redwood only for Sev1 but not for Sev2s? We want to limit noise.
[10:17] Nina: Absolutely — we can configure PD rules so only Sev1 pager escalations create PD incidents; Sev2 can create low-priority tickets or email notifications per your preference.
[10:25] Maya: Sounds good. We'll review the SOC2 and then set a date for the BCDR demo.
[10:30] Alex: Great. Next steps as we outlined — we'll follow up with the artifacts and schedule. Thanks everyone.
[10:36] Meeting end.

Notes on transcription: occasional speaker label noise; some technical terms may be transcribed approximately (e.g., 'KV cache' as 'K V cache' in places).
